newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-OECD sees no reason for Buba move on rates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-OECD sees no reason for Buba move on rates.

text.p: The Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development said on Tuesday conditions for low interest rates and economic growth in Germany would remain intact throughout this year and next.

The Paris-based forecasting group predicted in an annual report that Germany would exceed the strict deficit and debt targets for economic and monetary union (EMU), but that it would still qualify, as it satisfied the "spirit of Maastricht".

OECD economists at a news conference in Bonn declined to comment directly on the mark's weakness, one reason why the powerful Bundesbank has hinted that it could edge up a key interest rate, although it failed to do so on Tuesday.
"Our forecasts are for the period through 1998. During this time-frame we see no reason to change the stance on monetary policy," said Grant Kirkpatrick, head of the OECD's Germany group.
The OECD report predicted the German economy would expand 2.2 percent this year and that growth would accelerate to 2.8 percent next year, roughly in line with Bonn's own forecasts.
Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt welcomed the report's conclusions, saying "it confirms our expectation that the German economy is getting underway and employment will rise next year."

The OECD forecast Germany's total public sector deficit would fall to 3.2 percent of gross domestic product this year, but still exceeding the three percent ceiling in the Maastricht treaty, one of the key marks for entry into monetary union.

The report predicted that Germany's total debt would be 62 percent of GDP this year, exceeding the Maastricht limit of 60 percent. It said high debt levels were largely from the costs of unification and that Germany would still qualify for EMU.
"We would regard 3.2 percent as meeting the criteria," said Robert Price, director of the OECD's countries division.
The OECD economists pointed out that a long-term trend towards low debt and budget deficits and sound fiscal policy was more important than hitting the targets precisely.
"Germany is in the position to fulfil the spirit of the Maastricht Treaty on debt," said Kirkpatrick.
The OECD report also warned that some of the measures taken to cut budget deficits put German fiscal policy in conflict with longer-term goals of establishing sound state finances.
"Some of the ways in which the deficit has been contained -- such as the rise of social security charges -- have run contrary to the attainment of other longer run fiscal objectives," it said.

"A key policy question is whether it would be possible, or even desirable, in the case of deteriorating growth and employment prospects and associated further budget slippage, to tighten fiscal policy in the course of the year," it said.
An option such as raising excise taxes would be possible, but this could cause confusion over Bonn's overall tax strategy.
In its report, the OECD contradicts inflation hawks who see the mark's current weakness against the dollar as reason to raise interest rates to head off any pressure on prices.
It pointed out that the mark's decline from all-time highs against the dollar in 1995 was a proper adjustment that was having a positive impact on Germany's lacklustre economy.

"With forward rates in the money market showing little sign of any expected tightening of policy and inflation well under control, there is clearly neither the expectation nor justification for a tightening of stance," the report insisted.
Indeed, the central bank could still have scope to lower interest rates again if economic growth does not pick up in line with forecasts, the report continued.
The greatest risk to interest rate stability would be any sudden swings in foreign exchange rates, such as those seen in July and early August that raised eyebrows at the Bundesbank.

"There are two problems: the exchange rate level and the question of the pace of change," said Kirkpatrick. "We cannot say what the proper level is, but such rapid changes would create problems for any central bank."
The report gives the German government good marks for attained fiscal reforms, but said there is more to be done.

"A lot was achieved in the past year," said Dieter Menke, head of the OECD office in Bonn. "But it is important that current legislative proposals are enacted, namely tax reform and improvements on financial markets."

OECD economists said they did not expect any changes this year or next to Germany's tax system, nor did they expect a reduction in the solidarity surcharge on income tax bills that is used to finance the costs of German unification.
